lesson.title: The Simplest Living Cells: Life Without a Nucleus
lesson.summary: Bacteria and archaea run every core process of life using a cell design with no internal compartments, proving that a simple architecture can still be a wildly successful one.
lesson.body:
Cell theory holds that every living organism is built from cells, and that the cell is the smallest unit that can be considered fully alive. Prokaryotic cells put that claim to its simplest possible test. Bacteria and archaea, the two domains of life made of prokaryotic cells, carry out metabolism, growth, and reproduction using a design that lacks a nucleus and lacks the membrane-bound organelles found in eukaryotic cells. The word prokaryote reflects this directly: "pro" means before, and "karyon" refers to the nucleus, so a prokaryotic cell is, by definition, a cell that lacks a true, membrane-enclosed nucleus.

Despite the missing compartments, prokaryotic cells are far from disorganized. A single, usually circular chromosome of double-stranded DNA sits in a region of the cytoplasm called the nucleoid. Unlike the eukaryotic nucleus, the nucleoid has no membrane around it, so the DNA sits in direct contact with the rest of the cytoplasm. Ribosomes, the molecular machines that build proteins, are scattered freely through the cytoplasm rather than anchored to an endoplasmic reticulum, and they are smaller, classified as 70S, than the 80S ribosomes found in eukaryotic cells. Many bacteria also carry small extra loops of DNA called plasmids, which often carry genes such as antibiotic resistance and can be passed between cells independently of the main chromosome.

Outside the plasma membrane, most prokaryotic cells are reinforced by a rigid cell wall that maintains the cell's shape and keeps it from bursting or collapsing as water moves in and out. In true bacteria the wall is built largely from peptidoglycan, a mesh of sugars and short protein chains; archaea build their walls from different materials entirely, one of several biochemical differences that separates the two prokaryotic domains. Some species add a slimy outer capsule for extra protection, and many are motile thanks to flagella, whip-like propellers that rotate like a motor, a mechanism structurally different from the flagella found in some eukaryotic cells.

Size matters here as much as internal structure. A typical prokaryotic cell runs about one to five micrometers across, roughly ten to fifty times smaller than a typical eukaryotic cell. That small size gives the cell a very large surface area relative to its volume, meaning nutrients can diffuse in and wastes can diffuse out fast enough to keep the whole cell supplied without any need for internal membranes or organelles to shuttle materials around. Small size is not a limitation here; it is the reason the simple prokaryotic design works at all, a relationship examined more closely in the next chapter.

Escherichia coli, a bacterium living by the billions in the human gut, illustrates the model well. A single E. coli cell is about two micrometers long, carries a chromosome of roughly 4.6 million DNA base pairs, and under good conditions can divide about every twenty minutes. That combination of a compact genome, an efficient small-cell design, and rapid division has made prokaryotes the most numerous and widespread form of life on the planet, setting up a clear contrast with the larger, more compartmentalized eukaryotic cells covered next.
